chapter.name: The Age of Reorganisation
chapter.blurb: The breakup of the Maurya Empire, the Shungas, Satavahanas, Chedis, southern kingdoms, Indo-Greeks, Shakas and Kushanas and their art.

scope_in.item: The Kushanas and the art of Gandhara and Mathura

concepts.name: The breakup of the Maurya Empire: an age of reorganisation
concepts.description: The end of the Mauryas, new competing kingdoms and how they gained control.
concepts.idea: After the Mauryas, many kingdoms competed and the map of India was reorganised.
concepts.rule: The last Maurya emperor was assassinated around 185 BCE by his commander-in-chief Pushyamitra Shunga. The empire broke up and many earlier tributary kingdoms became independent. The weak northwest was exposed to invasions. Some scholars call the period the age of reorganisation. Kingdoms competed through matrimonial alliances or force, and border areas were important for safety. Dynasties from within the subcontinent included the Shungas, Chedis, Satavahanas, Cholas, Cheras and Pandyas; outsiders included the Indo-Greeks, Shakas and Kushanas.
concepts.example: A king might offer his daughter in marriage into a neighbouring royal family to cement an alliance.

concepts.name: The Shungas
concepts.description: Pushyamitra Shunga, the ashvamedha yajna, revival of Vedic rituals, Patanjali and Bharhut art.
concepts.idea: The Shungas revived Vedic rituals and patronised literature and art such as the Bharhut Stupa.
concepts.rule: Pushyamitra Shunga founded the Shunga dynasty in north and central India. He performed the ashvamedha yajna, in which a horse and soldiers wander freely and the lands it crosses unchallenged become part of the king's empire; a challenge leads to battle. His empire was smaller than the Maurya empire and was gone a century later. Vedic rituals revived while other schools flourished. Patanjali compiled the Yoga Sutras. The Shungas added carved railings and reliefs of the Buddha's life to the Bharhut Stupa in Madhya Pradesh.
concepts.example: The Bharhut railings carry carvings of Lakshmi, singers and dancers.

concepts.name: The Satavahanas
concepts.description: The Deccan dynasty, trade and coins, women in the dynasty, patronage and decline.
concepts.idea: The Satavahanas ruled the Deccan and grew rich from maritime trade and patronage of many schools.
concepts.rule: The Satavahanas ruled large parts of the Deccan from the 2nd century BCE, mostly in present Andhra Pradesh, Telangana and Maharashtra, with capitals at Amaravati and Pratishthana (Paithan). Their coins with ships show maritime trade. Agriculture flourished in the Krishna-Godavari system. Trade reached the Roman Empire; they exported spices, textiles and sandalwood and imported glass and ointments. Princes took mothers' names, as Gautamiputra Satakarni did. They were followers of Vasudeva but granted tax-free land to Vedic scholars, Jaina and Buddhist monks. The empire fragmented in the 3rd century CE.

concepts.name: The Chedis and Kharavela of Kalinga
concepts.description: Kalinga under the Chedis, Kharavela, the Hathigumpha inscription and rock-cut caves.
concepts.idea: Kharavela of Kalinga recorded his deeds on the Hathigumpha inscription and respected all sects.
concepts.rule: After the Mauryas, Kalinga rose under the Chedi dynasty. Kharavela was a devoted follower of Jain teachings, sometimes called the monk-king, but respected all schools. The Udayagiri-Khandagiri caves near Bhubaneswar were likely made for Jain monks and are examples of rock-cut architecture. The Hathigumpha inscription in Brahmi records his victories and welfare works year after year. He claims a council of ascetics and sages from a hundred regions and to be a respecter of every sect and repairer of every temple.
concepts.example: Kharavela claims to have defeated an alliance of south Indian kings, but the location is unknown.

concepts.name: Kingdoms of the south: Sangam Age, Cholas, Cheras and Pandyas
concepts.description: Sangam literature, the Silappadikaram, and the three southern kingdoms with their trade and achievements.
concepts.idea: The Cholas, Cheras and Pandyas flourished in the Sangam Age with rich literature and trade.
concepts.rule: Between the 2nd or 3rd century BCE and the 3rd century CE three powerful southern kingdoms, the Cheras, Cholas and Pandyas, flourished. The word sangam means association, here an assembly of poets, and Sangam literature is the oldest in south India. The Cholas (capital Uraiyur/Puhar) included Karikala, who built the Kallanai or Grand Anicut, still in use, making the Kaveri delta the rice bowl of the south. The Cheras (capital Vanji) traded spices, timber, ivory and pearls with Rome. The Pandyas (capital Madurai) were known for pearls and naval power. The Silappadikaram tells of Kannagi.
concepts.example: The Kallanai diverts water from the Kaveri and is still in use.

concepts.name: The Indo-Greeks and the Shakas
concepts.description: How Alexander's satraps became Indo-Greeks, cultural blending, the Heliodorus pillar and the Shaka calendar.
concepts.idea: Indo-Greeks blended Greek and Indian culture, and the Shakas gave India its national calendar.
concepts.rule: Satraps left by Alexander became independent as the Indo-Greeks and took over the northwest after the Mauryas. They were influenced by local culture, blending Greek and Indian elements in governance, art and language. The Heliodorus pillar near Vidisha, named after an Indo-Greek ambassador, praises Vasudeva as the god of gods. Indo-Greek coins were of gold, silver, copper and nickel, some with Vasudeva-Krishna and Lakshmi. The Shakas (Indo-Scythians) ruled from the 2nd century BCE to the 5th century CE and developed the Shaka Samvat calendar, adopted as the Indian National Calendar in 1957.
concepts.example: Dates on official publications are given in the Gregorian and Shaka Samvat eras.

concepts.name: The Kushanas and the art of Gandhara and Mathura
concepts.description: The Kushana empire and Kanishka, the Silk Route, the Gandhara and Mathura schools and cultural exchange.
concepts.idea: The Kushanas controlled the Silk Route and fostered the Gandhara and Mathura schools of art.
concepts.rule: The Kushanas came from Central Asia, probably in the 2nd century CE, and their empire stretched from Central Asia to northern India. Kanishka was probably the most powerful ruler; a headless statue bears the inscription 'great king, king of kings, son of God, Kanishka'. His coins show Buddha and Shiva with Nandi. They held large parts of the Silk Route. The Gandhara school used grey-black schist and blended Greco-Roman and Indian features. The Mathura school used red sandstone and showed Indian deities with fuller figures. The period also saw the composition of the Mahabharata and Ramayana.
concepts.example: Kanishka's coins show the Buddha with a Greek-script inscription.
